div.p: While multi-agent systems have been shown to significantly enhance the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various tasks and applications, the dense interaction between scaling agents potentially hampers their efficiency and diversity. To address these challenges, we draw inspiration from the sparse mixture-of-agents (SMoE) and propose a sparse mixture-of-agents (SMoA) framework to improve the efficiency and diversity of multi-agent LLMs. Unlike completely connected structures, SMoA introduces novel Response Selection and Early Stopping mechanisms to sparsify information flows among individual LLM agents, striking a balance between performance and efficiency. Additionally, inspired by the expert diversity principle in SMoE frameworks for workload balance between experts, we assign distinct role descriptions to each LLM agent, fostering diverse and divergent thinking. Extensive experiments on reasoning, alignment, and fairness benchmarks demonstrate that SMoA achieves performance comparable to traditional mixture-ofagents approaches but with significantly lower computational costs. Further analysis reveals that SMoA is more stable, has a greater capacity to scale, and offers considerable potential through hyper-parameter optimization.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020;Anil et al., 2023;Gan et al., 2023;Dubey et al., 2024) in recent years has significantly advanced in a series of NLP tasks, such as question answering (Wang et al., 2022;Tong et al., 2023;Jin et al., 2024a), knowledge discovery (Li et al., 2024a,b;Tan et al., 2024a) and dialogue systems (Li et al., 2022;Sun et al., 2024). While these powerful foundation models have been proven to benefit from extensive training data and larger model sizes, further scaling up these models is exceptionally costly, often requiring necessitating retraining on several trillion tokens (Zhang et al., 2024). To overcome this limitation, multiagent LLMs (Liang et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024b) have been explored, enabling LLM systems to incorporate multiple agents, each focused on distinct objectives and tasks. The layer-based structure (Liang et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024b) is one of the most fundamental strategies for implementing LLM-based multi-agent systems.

It involves instructing various LLMs to perform multi-agent debate (MAD) (Liang et al., 2023;Du et al., 2023) or discussion over multiple rounds to mimic human behavior in problem-solving. While effective in various applications, early layer-based methods (Liang et al., 2023) process user queries with only one agent each time, hindering their utilization in real-world scenarios. Recently, mixture-of-agents (MoA) (Zhang et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024b) has been devised, which uses multiple processors per layer to handle queries simultaneously for time efficiency purposes. An aggregator then synthesizes these references to produce a final answer.

Although MoA improves the time efficiency of multi-agent LLMs, it still faces significant challenges. The first issue is the high token computational cost. While MoA reduces processing time for user queries, its simultaneous processing nature increases overall computational demands, limiting scalability (Qian et al., 2024;Jin et al., 2024b) and severely undermining the token economy of existing multi-agent systems (Wang et al., 2024a). The second challenge is the lack of diverse thinking among LLM agents. Unlike MAD, which explicitly encourages different viewpoints, MoA relies on agents generating responses based on previous iterations, leading to homogenization and reduced performance in tasks requiring divergent thinking.

To overcome the limitations of MoA and enhance the utility of multi-agent LLMs, we propose Sparse Mixture-of-Agents (SMoA), inspired by the design of sparse mixture-of-experts (SMoE) (Han et al., 2015;Shazeer et al., 2016). Unlike fully connected structures, SMoA introduces sparsity in agent interactions through two novel agents: the Judge LLM, which selects high-quality responses for the next round, and the Moderator LLM, which controls the information flow and determines when to end it. This reduces unnecessary data processing, balancing performance with efficiency and enabling better scalability. Moreover, drawing inspiration from the expert diversity principle (Lepikhin et al.;Jiang et al., 2024a) which is commonly applied in SMoE to balance workload, we assign distinct role descriptions to each LLM agent, facilitating diverse and divergent thinking in their problem-solving process.

Previous multi-agent LLMs typically focus on one or two tasks (Liang et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024b), thus failing to obtain a comprehensive evaluation and understanding. In this work, we conduct extensive experiments across alignment, reasoning, safety, and fairness benchmarks to thoroughly evaluate various multi-agent LLM strategies. Our results show that SMoA performs comparably to MoA with much less computational costs. And MoA and SMoA are more stable and reliable than MAD in real-world problem-solving. Further analysis reveals that SMoA is more efficient, promotes diverse thinking, and has greater potential for scalability compared to MoA.
In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We identify key limitations in existing multiagent LLM frameworks and propose a novel SMoA architecture to address them.
• Through extensive experiments across various tasks, we demonstrate that SMoA achieves performance comparable to MoA while using significantly fewer computational resources.
• We provide further analysis, offering insights into the comparison of different multi-agent methods and highlighting the advantages of SMoA.
2 Related Work

div.head: Multi-agent LLMs
div.p: Multi-agent LLMs aim to explore the utilization of multiple LLMs as agents and direct them to work collaboratively to solve given problems. One line of work is layer-based multi-agent methods (Liang et al., 2023;Du et al., 2023;Chan et al.), in which multiple LLMs are prompted to debate or discuss with each other and defend their own response. Additionally, there are some works that propose mixture-of-agents, to guide various LLMs to collaborate with each other by referring to others' responses and generating their own continuation (Zhang et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023b;Wang et al., 2024b). Based on these two architectures, some other more complex structures are proposed to mimic human workflows in various domains, such as code generation (Hong et al.) and biomedical reasoning (Tang et al.).

div.head: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
div.p: The key idea in SMoE (Shazeer et al., 2016;Chen et al., 2023;He et al., 2023He et al., , 2024) ) is to activate only a few experts per input, significantly reducing computational costs compared to the traditional MoE models. Several improvements have been proposed to enhance the performance and stability of sparse MoE models. Routing techniques such as dynamic routing (Rosenbaum et al., 2018) and Hash-based routing (Roller et al., 2021) help optimize which experts are activated, ensuring efficient resource use. Furthermore, balancing load across experts, which is first proposed by Fedus et al. (2022), addresses issues like expert imbalance, which can lead to the underutilization of certain experts and over-specialization of others. In this work, we borrow insights from SMoE to sparse the information flow between each layer in SMoA and diversify agent LLMs using role-playing.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: In this section, we begin by providing a preliminary introduction to MoA. Based on this, we illuminate the principles and details for designing our SMoA.
Figure 2 presents the overall structure of SMoA.

div.head: Preliminary: Mixture-of-Agents
div.p: While MoA structure for multi-agent LLMs system has been adopted by various previous studies, in this work we follow the implementation and definition from Wang et al. (2024b). In their work, they assign LLMs to two distinct roles, proposers and aggregators, in their collaboration process. Proposers focus on generating useful reference responses for each other while aggregators are models proficient in synthesizing responses from other models into a single, high-quality output. Specifically, the structure of MoA consist of l layers and each layer-i contains n LLMs as proposers, so we use P i,1 , P i,2 , ..., P i,n , to denote them. In one layer, each proposer P i,j processes the input text and generates its continuation as a reference for the next layer. Given an input x 1 , the output of i-th MoA layer y i can be formulated as:

div.head: Sparse Mixture-of-Agents
div.p: To improve MoA structures and achieve better performance-efficiency balance, we draw inspiration from the concepts of SMoE. It highlights dynamically selecting only a subset of experts using the gate function to process an input, which optimizes computational efficiency while maintaining model performance. Motivated by this, we devise two new roles in our SMoA architecture:

• Judge should conduct a comprehensive assessment and comparison to the responses generated by each processor, filtering out those in low quality and only passing a subset of high-quality and reasonable responses to the next round.

• Moderator is the agent responsible for controlling the forward process of each processor. It should make the decision to end the processors' forward process when the multiple processors reach a consensus for efficiency consideration. Based on the two new agents we designed, we further propose Response Selection (Section 3.2.1) and Early Stopping (Section 3.2.2) to fully utilize them in MoA optimization.

div.head: Response Selection with Judge
div.p: In the MoA framework, while each processor in a layer generates its own continuation for a given input, it becomes crucial to decide which responses should be passed to the subsequent layer or used in the final output generation. To address this challenge, SMoA introduces a judge agent J, which plays a central role in response selection. J evaluates the outputs generated by the LLMs in the current layer and determines which responses are most suitable to advance to the next round.

Specifically, we borrow insights from the Top-K selection in SMoE (Shazeer et al., 2016). Given an input x i and the generated response candidates P i,1 (x i ), ..., P i,n (x i ), we prompt the judge J to select the best k responses and concatenate them as the input for the next iteration:
div.formula: ) y i = ⊕ k j=1 [P ′ i,j (x i )] + x 1 , x i+1 = y i , (4
div.p: ) where k controls the sparsity of the whole agent network. By introducing Response Selection, SMoA significantly reduces noise and enhances the overall efficiency of information flowing among layers, particularly in cases where the number of LLMs in each layer is large. This method enables SMoA to balance the trade-off between efficiency in generation and the quality of the final output, leveraging the great potential of LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) to guide the response forward process.

div.head: Early Stopping with Moderator
div.p: In the MoA framework, layers of LLMs generate multiple responses iteratively, passing refined outputs to subsequent layers. This process is controlled by a fixed round number. However, in some cases, continuing the process across all layers may not be necessary if a high-quality response is achieved early on or most of the processors achieve a consensus. While several previous studies (Liu et al., 2023) propose rule-based methods to address it (e.g., stop when the output answers from most agents are the same), there is still a lack of a general and dynamic approach that can handle various tasks and applications. To manage this, SMoA introduces a moderator agent M that can dynamically assess the state of outputs at each layer and decide whether to stop the process earlier, effectively implementing an early stopping mechanism.

div.p: here T rue/F alse means whether to stop the iteration and generate the final response. In our prompt for the moderator agent, we list fine-grained aspects for the moderator to check for early stopping decision-making, including quality, consensus level, and contentiousness degree (Chang, 2024). The early stopping method, therefore, serves as a dynamic controller to apply fine-grained moderation to the collaboration process. This adds flexibility and makes SMoA a more efficient and adaptable framework, capable of delivering high-quality results while minimizing unnecessary computations.

div.head: Role Playing with Processor
div.p: Another key mechanism in SMoE is the diversity principles among experts, to ensure the robustness and load balancing for the whole network. In SMoA, we also borrow this insight and adopt role-playing (Wang et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023a), a widely adopted technique in personalized dialogue to improve the diversity among each processor.

Specifically, we produce diverse role descriptions based on certain dataset description D and task requirement T , and assign these role descriptions to every proposer as their system prompt in candidate response generation:

4 Experiment 4.1 Experiment Settings

Benchmarks We conduct evaluation in a wide range of tasks to measure each method's alignment level, reasoning capability and safety and fairness degree. For alignment level evaluation, we use the Just-Eval (Lin et al., 2023) benchmark, which contains diverse samples from 5 alignment datasets: (1) AlpacaEval2 (Li et al., 2023c), (2) MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), (3) LIMA (Zhou et al., 2024), (4) HH-RLHF-redteam (Ganguli et al., 2022) and ( 5) MaliciousInstruct (Huang et al.). We follow Lin et al. (2023) and use the GPT-4o to rate the responses for all the samples. For reasoning, we use the Massive Multitask Agent Understanding (MMAU) benchmark (Yin et al., 2024), which involves challenging reasoning tasks including math understanding, tool-using and code contests. Additionally, we also adopt CEB (Wang et al., 2024c), a conversation dataset focusing on the examination of responses' fairness(e.g., toxicity and stereotype).

div.head: Compared Method
div.p: We compare the following multi-agent and ensemble methods in experiments: • Self-Consistency (SC) (Wang et al.) follows a sample-then-vote pattern and leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer.
• Mixture-of-Agent (MoA) is the fully-connected multi-agent framework as we introduced in Section 3.1. In our experiment, we follow the implementation of (Wang et al., 2024b).
• Multi-agent Debating (MAD) (Liang et al., 2023) based on the original MoA.

Implementation Details In our main experiment, we construct each multi-agent and ensemble method by using only open-source models to achieve reproduced and fair comparison. We follow (Wang et al., 2024b) and adopt: Qwen1.5-72B-Chat (Bai et al., 2023), Qwen2-72B-instruct (Yang et al., 2024), WizardLM-8x22B (Xu et al., 2023), dbrx-instruct (Team et al., 2024). Besides, we also introduce two more powerful closed-source models from OpenAI: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, for a thorough evaluation. For MoA and SMoA, we set 4 and 2 to the processor number and layer number. For SMoA, we set the selection response number k to 2. We also conduct further analysis on these hyperparameters in Section 5. More implementation details can be found in Appendix B.

div.head: Main Result
div.p: Overall Comparison We begin by comparing the performance of different methods in each dataset (Table 1, 2 and 3). For Just-Eval, SC, MoA and SMoA significantly improve the baseline performance, while MAD results in a performance decline. Notably, SMoA and MoA exhibit comparable results in the alignment task, even when compared with the powerful GPT-4o model. In the MMAU dataset, SC stands out with exceptional performance, considerably boosting the baselines. MoA and SMoA also provide consistent improve-ments, whereas MAD fails to deliver positive results. For the CEB dataset, SMoA emerges as the best for reducing baselines' toxicity and stereotypes, achieving the best results in three out of the four baseline LLMs. MoA and SC follow as the second and third best methods, while MAD again decreases baseline performance. In summary: (1) MoA and SMoA offer consistent and comparable improvements across all three tasks. (2) SC outperforms MoA and SMoA in reasoning tasks but falls behind in alignment and fairness. (3) MAD is the least effective method, leading to performance drops in almost every task.

div.head: Comparison of multi-agent methods.
div.p: To gain a more fine-grained and deeper understanding of each multi-agent method, we provide a direct comparison in Figures 3a and 3b with Qwen2-72B-Instruct. In Figure 3a, we analyze alignment and fairness attributes using the Just-Eval and CEB datasets. Both MoA and SMoA improve the singleagent baseline in terms of depth and engagement, while also reducing stereotypes and toxicity. Interestingly, we find that although MAD performs competitively in terms of helpfulness and safety, it underperforms the baseline in all other aspects. We attribute this to the binary nature of debate, which may limit diverse thinking in real-world scenarios.

In Figure 3b, we evaluate the reasoning capabilities of each method across three MMAU sub- sets. We notice MoA consistently enhances the single LLM baseline's performance across all tasks. While SMoA's improvement is slightly less than MoA's, it still delivers consistent enhancement. However, MAD's impact on the baseline is mixed: it significantly boosts math understanding but reduces performance in the tool and code subsets.
Based on these observations, we conclude that layer-based architectures (such as MoA and SMoA) are generally more stable and reliable than the debate-based approach for multi-agent LLMs.

div.head: Further Analysis
div.p: In this section, we conduct in-depth analyses to understand SMoA thoroughly and provide further insights for future works. We summarize our findings and conclusions below.

Response number is an important hyperparameter in SMoA. We conducted an ablation study on Response Selection, with the results presented in Table 4. The results suggest that while Response Selection improves efficiency, it seems to also reduce performance in MMAU and CEB. To better understand its impact, we performed a hyperparameter analysis on the selected response number k. As shown in Figure 5, the model's performance exhibits a clear pattern that initially improves as k increases (when k = 1, 2, 3), then declines (when k = 4). Notably, the model achieved optimal per- formance across all three datasets when k = 3, indicating a balance between the informativeness and quality of the selected reference responses. These findings emphasize that the number of selected responses is a critical hyper-parameter in SMoA, essential for balancing efficiency and performance.

Early Stopping sacrifices a little performance for a huge efficiency boost. As shown in Table 4, the ablation results for Early Stopping reveal a slight performance decline across three datasets when this mechanism is removed. However, there is a remarkable increase in costs, with the average rising from 1.75 to 3.70 per dataset. These findings underscore the significant effectiveness of Early Stopping in enhancing the efficiency of SMoA, at the cost of sacrificing a little performance. Additionally, we observe that removing Early Stopping results in higher costs than the original MoA (3.70 vs. 3.25), which is due to the additional prompt tokens required for Role-playing and Response Selection. This further hints at the importance of Early Stopping in the SMoA framework.

Divergent thinking brought by Role-playing benefits both the reasoning capability and fairness of multi-agent LLMs. When the Roleplaying module is removed (Table 4), we observe a significant performance drop in MMAU and CEB, which are closely related to the LLMs' reasoning and fairness capabilities. This suggests that the divergent and diverse thinking fostered by the roleplaying process greatly benefits multi-agent LLMs in these areas. This finding is also consistent with previous studies that focus on reasoning (Wang et al., 2022) and fairness (Han et al., 2021; Saun-MMAU CEB Just-Eval Cost MoA 25.95 6.22 4.91 3.25 SMoA 24.57 5.84 4.91 1.75 w/o RS 26.37 5.68 4.90 2.11 w/o ES 25.43 5.78 4.92 3.70 w/o RP 23.70 6.12 4.90 1.61 SMoA shows greater potential for scaling up.

Scalability is a crucial factor in evaluating multiagent LLM systems (Qian et al., 2024). To address this, we conducted a scaling analysis to compare SMoA with MoA in terms of their ability to scale. Specifically, we incorporated additional LLM processors (deepseek-llm-67b (Bi et al., 2024), Llama-3-70b-chat (Dubey et al., 2024), and WizardLM-2-8x22B (Xu et al., 2024)) and monitored the performance and token cost trends as the number of

In contrast, SMoA shows better efficiency and maintains more acceptable token utilization with the increasing number of processors. Moreover, SMoA's performance surpasses that of MoA as the number of processors grows, despite using significantly fewer tokens. These findings highlight SMoA's potential for scaling efficiently with more agents. SMoA sits at the performance-efficiency frontier. In Figure 4, we plot the performance scores against the average inference costs for the MMAU dataset, helping to identify cost-effective models that deliver high performance without excessive expenses. The chart reveals a "Pareto front", where certain models achieve an optimal balance between cost and performance. Models closer to this front are more desirable, as they offer better value by delivering higher performance at lower costs. No-tably, SMoA achieves the best performance while utilizing significantly fewer tokens. To ensure a fair comparison with similar computational costs, we adjust the number of processor agents for SMoA and MoA, and introduce SMoA-Pro by increasing both the number of agents and selected responses. Overall, we conclude that SMoA's configuration leads to the performance-efficiency frontier.

div.head: Case Study
div.p: We present an example in Table 6 to more clearly illustrate the effectiveness of Response Selection and Early Stopping. As shown, the responses from Qwen2-72B-Instruct and Qwen1.5-72B-Chat are correct, while those from Mixtral-8x22B-Instruct-v0.1 and dbrx-instruct are incorrect. Notably, the judge agent successfully selects the correct responses and filters out the incorrect ones, preventing potential misguidance during the aggregation process. Additionally, the moderator agent triggers Early Stopping based on the current response states, enhancing SMoA's efficiency in both time and computational resources. Due to the space limitation, we put more and completed cases into Appendix D. In all, SMoA performs well in identifying reasoning error (Tong et al., 2024;An et al., 2023) and filtering out unsafe content (Tan et al., 2024b;Beigi et al., 2024b) or misinformation (Jiang et al., 2024b;Yang et al., 2023;Beigi et al., 2024a) and moderating the information exchange process.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper presents the SMoA architecture, designed to enhance the efficiency and diversity of multi-agent LLM systems. Our approach leverages sparsity to optimize the fully connected structure commonly used in current layer-based multi-agent methods. Through extensive evaluation across various benchmarks and models, we provide a comprehensive comparison and analysis of existing multiagent approaches. Additionally, further analysis reveals that SMoA not only improves efficiency and fosters diverse thinking but also offers greater scalability potential compared to the original MoA.

div.head: Limitation
div.p: In this work, we introduce sparsity to the layerbased multi-agent LLMs, which is a fundamental structure in multi-agent LLM systems. We also notice there are some network-based multi-agent structures emerging recently (Zhuge et al.;Qian et al., 2024). Due to space limitations, we don't apply our method to these methods and leave this for future works. Additionally, while our SMoA reduces the input token for each processor, all processors are activated for reference generation. One promising direction for future research is exploring effective strategies for sparse activation for layerbased multi-agent LLMs.

div.head: Ethical Statement
div.p: In our study, we follow the ethical considerations and principles below: • Transparency: We strive to ensure that our multiagent systems operate transparently, providing clear explanations of their functionalities, capabilities, and limitations. Users should understand how these models generate outputs and the potential implications of their use.

• Accountability: We acknowledge our responsibility for the behavior of our LLMs and the outcomes of their interactions. We commit to monitoring and addressing any issues that arise from the deployment of our models, including unintended consequences or harmful outputs.

• Fairness and Non-Discrimination: We aim to minimize biases in our multi-agent LLMs, ensuring that they treat all users equitably, regardless of race, gender, ethnicity, religion, or other characteristics. Our models are designed to promote inclusivity and diversity in their interactions.

• Privacy and Data Protection: We prioritize the privacy and security of user data. Our systems do not store personal information without consent, and we implement robust measures to protect any data that may be processed during interactions.

• Safety and Harm Reduction: We are committed to preventing the dissemination of harmful content and ensuring the safety of users interacting with our multi-agent systems. Our models are designed with safety protocols to reduce the risk of generating harmful or misleading information.
• Collaboration and Community Engagement:

We recognize the importance of collaboration with stakeholders, including researchers, practitioners, and the communities affected by our technology. We seek feedback and insights to continuously improve our models and their ethical deployment.

• Sustainability: We are committed to the responsible use of resources in developing and maintaining our multi-agent LLMs. This includes considering the environmental impact of computational resources and promoting practices that support sustainability.

div.head: B More Implement Details
div.p: In our main experiment, we construct each multi-agent and ensemble method by using only open-source models to achieve reproduced and fair comparison. We follow (Wang et al., 2024b) and adopt: Qwen1.5-72B-Chat (Bai et al., 2023), Qwen2-72B-instruct (Yang et al., 2024), WizardLM-8x22B (Xu et al., 2023), dbrx-instruct (Team et al., 2024). Besides, we also introduce two more powerful closed-source models from OpenAI: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, for a thorough evaluation. For MoA and SMoA, we set 4 and 2 to the processor number and layer number. For SMoA, we set the selection response number k to 2. We also conduct further analysis on these hyper-parameters in Section 5. For MAD, we follow the original paper and set the number of debating agents to be 2. For SC, we set the diverse reasoning path to be 4, which leads to a comparable computational cost with our method. We use 0.7 as the temperature to sample more diverse response from LLMs. All the experiments with open-source LLMs are based on together.aifoot_0 's corresponding APIs.

The game is played on a rectangular court that is divided by a net. Here 2019s a breakdown of the basic rules and gameplay:### Court and Equipment-Court: The badminton court measures 44 feet (13.4 meters) long and 17 feet (5.18 meters) wide for singles, and 20 feet (6.1 meters) wide for doubles. The net is 6.1 meters (20 feet) long and 67 centimeters (26.4 inches) deep. It is placed at a height of 6.1 meters (2 feet) at the edges and 6.1 meters (5 feet 11.5 inches) at the center.-Racquets: Badminton racquets are lightweight, usually weighing between 85 and 140 grams (3 to 5 ounces). They have a long handle and a small round head with an open hoop covered by a network of strings.-Shuttlecock (Birdie): This is the ball used in badminton, consisting of 16 goose or nylon feathers attached to a rounded cork base. Synthetic shuttlecocks are also common.### Objective of the GameThe objective of badminton is to hit the shuttlecock over the net in such a way that your opponent is unable to return it. A point is scored when the shuttlecock lands within the opponent's court or if they fail to return the shuttlecock correctly.### Scoring-21-point system: Professional and tournament matches use a 21-point system. A game is won by the first player or team to reach 21 points, leading by a minimum of two points. If the score reaches 20-20, the game continues until one side has a two-point lead. A match is typically best of three games. Maintaining a high level of consistency while waiting for an opportunity to hit a winning shot is crucial.Badminton is not only a game of skill and strategy but also one that requires physical agility and quick reflexes.
